newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Birch says NZ markets react maturely to election.
newsitem.headline: Birch says NZ markets react maturely to election.

text.p: New Zealand Finance Minister Bill Birch said on Monday that financial markets had responded maturely to the inconclusive general election outcome.
"I think the financial markets have responded in a mature way," Birch told Reuters.

"There is a pretty strong appreciation in the markets about the role of the caretaker government... During the caretaker period nothing changes, the policies simply continue as they are while negotiations... continue."

Saturday's election returned the governing conservative National Party as the biggest in parliament, but well short of a majority. Nationalist New Zealand First holds the balance of power between National and the centre-left Labour party.

Asked about the possibility of prolonged political stalemate, Birch said: "I can understand the market's apprehension about that but I think the election result indicated strong support for the direction in which the economy is going. That will be reassuring, and during the caretaker period there'll be no change in policies."
Birch added: "The outcome of the election was very positive for those who were worried that suddenly the economy was going to be turned on its head."

New Zealand First policy includes a 24.9 percent limit on foreign investment in "strategic" assets such as utilities, and a change to the Reserve Bank's 0-2 percent inflation target. It wants to make the bank aim for inflation below the average of New Zealand's trading partners.
Birch refused to be drawn on whether National was prepared to explore a widening of the inflation band in negotiations with New Zealand First.
On foreign investment policy, Birch said the position of New Zealand First was not the only one to be taken into account.
Free-market Act New Zealand, with eight MPs, and centrist United, with one, are expected to back the government. Labour also favours an open foreign investment regime.
Birch said he expected a "period of relative calm" under National's caretaker government.
Asked if National would insist on his remaining finance minister in negotiations with New Zealand First, Birch said it would be a matter for Prime Minister Jim Bolger.
"I think we just have to wait for the chemistry of the negotiations to unfold...I would hope that I'd be playing a prominent role," he said.
Labour leader Helen Clark said last week that obtaining the finance portfolio for Labour's Michael Cullen would be a non- negotiable point if her party entered coalition talks with New Zealand First.
